sweep_summary: Tariana (tari1256) is not in the catalog. All 8 works with stress in the title are Glottolog keyword noise: they match 'pauses' (evidently through Aikhenvald 1996 'Words, phrases, pauses and boundaries', a genuine Tariana/Baniwa paper) and concern Dutch/English discourse production, German parentheticals, Japanese verse, Korean boundaries, interpreting, autism and speech synthesis; none is about Tariana or word stress (Crossref/ISCA records checked and saved).org holds an open copy of Aikhenvald 2001, Dicionário Tariana-Português (Boletim MPEG Antropologia 17(1)), whose introduction states first-hand that stress is contrastive (díka 'he laughs' vs di-ká 'he sees'), that enclitics bear a second stress, and whose kinship tables show vocatives formed by stress shift — saved and quoted (p. 14); (2) the on-disk scanned of Dixon & Aikhenvald 1999 The Amazonian Languages gives Aikhenvald's areal chapter statement that Tariana has pitch accent (a low-high distinction) with a 'Tucano' accent, and the Arawak chapter lists 'Ta' among North Arawak pitch accent languages (excerpts saved). The best statement, Aikhenvald 2003 A Grammar of Tariana pp. 37-39 (per Wikipedia's paraphrase: primary stress on one of the last three syllables, penultimate most common, long vowels always stressed, roots underlyingly stressed, prefixes unstressed), is paywalled (Cambridge Core; Google Books blocked; no HathiTrust/archive.org copy) and is the high-priority acquisition. Tariana is absent from WALS stress features 14A-17A.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent is lexically contrastive (minimal pairs such as díka 'he laughs' vs diká 'he sees', dictionary p. 14; Le tariana p. 4) and realised as a pitch-type accent (author's own characterisation: contrastive, of a pitch type, attributed to Tucano influence). Each phonological word has one primary stress; long and nasal vowels are always stressed. Placement details (per the grammar's §2.3, which I could only read second-hand via Wikipedia's paraphrase of pp. 37-39): primary stress falls within the last three syllables, penultimate being most common in monomorphemic words, with antepenultimate and final also occurring; roots carry underlying stress, prefixes are unstressed, suffixes are lexically stressed or unstressed.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress exists and is obligatory on enclitics (p. xvii); 'enclitics which, unlike suffixes, have a secondary stress' (Aikhenvald 1999 Tariana Texts p. 17; dictionary 2001 p. 14 likewise). Vowel reduction occurs in syllables preceding a secondary stress (§2.3.5, second-hand).
new_statements.exceptions: Nasal vowels and long vowels are always stressed (p. xvii). Considerable inter-speaker variation in pronunciation; stress shift is a morphological device in some kinship vocatives (Tables 3.3-3.4, pp. 70-71, per Contents).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word: accent (with vowel harmony, aspiration, nasalisation) delimits phonological-word boundaries; enclitics form a larger unit carrying secondary stress. Examples record actual consultant pronunciation (Santa Rosa variety unless Periquitos is indicated).
new_statements.identity_note: Aikhenvald's grammar and dictionary describe the Wamiarikune Tariana of Santa Rosa (with Periquitos forms flagged), Iauaretê area, Brazil; the grammar's Appendix (pp. 620-629) covers dialect differences and Kumandene Tariana is treated separately in Aikhenvald 2014. All are under the language-level code tari1256; no separate dialect glottocodes checked.

[...] Muitas categorias verbais e nominais são expressadas com enclíticos que, ao contrário dos sufixos, tem um segundo acento; não há processos fonológicos que se aplique através das fronteiras clíticas.
new_statements.translation: Stress is contrastive — another consequence of Tukano influence. Stress is marked on every headword, for example di-ká 'he sees; to see', díka 'he laughs; to laugh'. [...] Many verbal and nominal categories are expressed by enclitics which, unlike suffixes, carry a second stress; there are no phonological processes that apply across clitic boundaries.
new_statements.citation: Aikhenvald, Alexandra Y. (with Cândido Brito, Leonardo Brito, Ismael Brito, Olívia Brito, Graciliano Sanchez Brito, Jovino Brito, José Luiz Sanchez Brito & Rafael da Silva Brito). 2001. Dicionário Tariana-Português e Português-Tariana. Boletim do Museu Paraense Emílio Goeldi, Série Antropologia 17(1). Belém: MPEG.
new_statements.reading: Tariana word stress is lexically contrastive (minimal pair díka vs di-ká), i.e. not fixed; it is realised as pitch accent (low-high) per Aikhenvald 1999 ch. 14 §4.1 and Table 14.2 ('pitch accent: yes' for Tariana). The dictionary gives no placement rule; the fuller statement (primary stress on one of the last three syllables, penultimate default, long vowels always stressed, roots underlyingly stressed, prefixes unstressed) is in Aikhenvald 2003 pp. 37-39, which could not be opened. Recommended coding for a new catalog record: lexical/unpredictable stress (right-edge three-syllable window), pitch accent realisation, with Aikhenvald 2003 to be acquired as the deciding source.

sources.locator: p. 14 (Introdução, §1; extracted text; enclitic remark line 440); Tabelas 5-7 pp. 42-43
sources.note: Introduction, section 1 (phonology), p. 14: stress ('acentuação') is contrastive, attributed to Tukano influence; stress is marked on every headword; minimal pair di-ká 'he sees; to see' vs díka 'he laughs; to laugh'. Also p. 14: enclitics, unlike suffixes, carry a second stress. Kinship tables 5-7 (pp. 42-43) show vocative forms derived by stress shift (nu-teduá-ru -> nu-tedua-rú; nu-nídua -> nu-niduá). No general placement rule is stated in the dictionary.

sources.note: Second-hand paraphrase: pitch accent language; primary and secondary stress; long vowels always stressed, most nasal vowels too; primary stress falls on one of the last three syllables, penultimate most common in monomorphemic words (dúpu 'lizard'), antepenultimate (képira 'bird') and final (yapuratú) also occur; all roots have underlying stress; prefixes unstressed; suffixes stressed or unstressed; stressed suffixes generally yield penultimate stress (máwi -> mawípi).

sources.quote: Pitch accent and intonation patterns in Tariana and in the Maku languages display striking similarities to Tucano, hence the "Tucano" accent in Tariana. [...] 4.1 Pitch accent. Pitch accent (a low-high distinction) is a property of all the languages spoken in the Vaupés. It is also found in Baniwa and Kurripako (e.g. Valadares 1994)
sources.locator: pp. 405-407 (§3 list item 2; §4.1 Pitch accent; Table 14.2)
sources.note: pp. 405-407: Tariana's pitch accent and intonation patterns 'display striking similarities to Tucano, hence the Tucano accent in Tariana'; §4.1 'Pitch accent (a low-high distinction) is a property of all the languages spoken in the Vaupés'; Table 14.2 codes Tariana 'pitch accent: yes'. Classifies the word-prosodic system as pitch accent (L/H); no placement rule.
